newsitem.title: TAIWAN: South Korea challenging Taiwan's cargo ranking.
newsitem.headline: South Korea challenging Taiwan's cargo ranking.

text.p: Taiwan said on Tuesday that its container port at Kaohsiung ranked as the world's third largest in 1995, but experts warned that South Korea's Pusan could usurp the ranking unless Taiwan allows links to China's top ports.
Kaohsiung, Taiwan's big southern port, processed about five million TEU (20-foot container equivalents) in 1995, up 3.1 percent from 1994, the government's statistics director said.
That put Kaohsiung a distant third behind Hong Kong's 12.6 million TEUs and Singapore's 11.8 million.

Kaohsiung's position is being challenged by both the world number four, Rotterdam, whose 4.8 million TEU was up 5.7 percent from 1994, and number five Pusan, whose 4.5 million TEUs reflected a dramatic 40.2 percent jump over 1994.

Taiwan freight dealers said South Korea's fast expansion in container shipping could knock Kaohsiung out of third place within two years unless Taiwan revitalises its sluggish economy and increases transshipments with China.
Taiwan, seen by China as a renegade province, has banned direct shipping links with the communist mainland since a civil war divided them in 1949.
Freight dealers said Kaohsiung would see immediate growth if China and Taiwan could agree on transshipments between it and the mainland ports of Shanghai and Tianjin.
Beijing has issued rules allowing direct links with its southeastern ports at Fuzhou and Xiamen, but actual sailings have yet to take place.
Freight dealers said those two relatively minor ports were not able to give Kaohsiung the container growth it needs.
"Only major ports like Shanghai and Tianjin can give Taiwan a major boost," one dealer said.

Dealers said they expected direct transshipments to start within a few months, although Taiwan will not allow any direct link it perceives as undermining the sovereignty of its exiled Republic of China government.
Chinese shipments to Taiwan now must transit Hong Kong and would arrive two or three days earlier if routed directly.

Richard Yu of Taiwan's Yang Ming Marine said Taiwan container shippers were well-placed to grab a portion of China's trade shipments from Hong Kong because of the island's excellent ports and facilities, offering big savings to customers.
Taiwan has proposed to establish "offshore transshipment centres" at Kaohsiung and three other ports from which ships flying third-country flags could sail directly to China.
China has issued rules limiting such shipments to vessels owned by Taiwan or mainland interests, regardless of what flag they fly.
Freight dealers said Taiwan is able to provide China with cheaper and faster container transshipment services, which would boost the mainland's international trade competitiveness.
